texty: The turf wall settles year by year, Anna, its grass roof folding back into the ground the forefathers took it from. Othila is that slow return of what was built to what holds it. You stand where the old line goes green again.

The frost is off the grass on that old wall now, and you wake to find the light already grey in the room, come while you slept. Dagaz is that turn from dark to day you never catch happening, only after. The night gave way and no one was watching. Was it the last hour of dark that changed, or the first of light?

The ewe stands still in the green field while the lamb rocks on legs it has never used before. Berkana is that first standing done under something that does not move away. The ground holds, and the small thing finds the grass beneath its feet. You are the field now, Anna, steady where the new step is taken.

The phone rings, and a voice carries the words you have waited for across the quiet room. Then everything falls away but the sound of that voice. Ansuz is the moment a message finds the ear it was meant for — will you hold it as spoken, or ask it to say more?

There, at the foot of the rowan, one root grips the bare stone where nothing should hold. The trunk leans in the wind off the field but never goes all the way down. This is what Eihwaz does, Anna, it keeps a thing standing that the weather has worked at for years. The rowan stays where it was planted.

The distance between the two horses holds steady while the slope steepens beneath them. Ehwaz is that matched stride, the way one animal reads the other and neither pulls ahead. Their breath falls into the same rhythm as the path narrows. You are climbing with another close at your side.

The doorway stays calm, Anna, while the wind tears at the grass on the far side of the wall. That turf bank is Algiz, the standing thing that takes the weather so a quiet space can hold behind it. Everything outside moves, and the still air by the threshold does not. What are you keeping sheltered in that stillness?

The bird on the rock does not lift, and the water below holds every cloud without a ripple. This is Isa, the cold hold that stops a thing mid-motion and keeps it there. What have you let go this still?

The walls of the room stay where they were, but the grey has left them and they hold a pale gold now. This is Dagaz, the moment the dark and the light change places without anything moving. The still thing you kept has not stirred, only the light on it has turned.

The whole valley lies under grey until the sun cracks it open, and then it is only this: light glinting on the wet stones at your feet. Sowilo is that sudden clearing, when seeing gathers to one bright point. Which stone holds the glint you keep coming back to?

The phone rings across the grey kitchen, and a voice says the thing you have waited weeks to hear, and then the whole room is only that sound. Ansuz is the word arriving from further off than you can see, gathering to one steady line. The rest of the morning falls away behind it. You are standing with the receiver still warm against your ear.

The slope keeps sliding, loose stone over loose stone, and one root threads through it all and does not give. Eihwaz is that hold beneath the falling, Anna, the thing that stays when everything above it moves. The scree settles against it and rests. Which stone has stopped sliding because something under it held?

See the single split in the rowan's bark, low down where the wind works hardest. Eihwaz is the wood that gives a little and holds, root deep in the cold ground beneath the farmhouse. You stand at its base, in the shade it keeps.

Two horses climb the track above the farmhouse, keeping the same pace over the stones. Ehwaz is that matched stride, neither one pulling ahead, neither falling back. You ride the near one, the other close at your knee.

The egg lies whole in the nest, warm through, and nothing of what waits inside shows on the smooth shell. Ingwaz is that gathering held quiet before it breaks open in its own hour. You sit beside the nest, hands still, keeping the warmth.

You stand at the thorn hedge, close enough that the barbs catch your sleeve. Thurisaz is the edge that lets nothing through without taking something first. Every gap in the branches asks a price of skin or patience before it opens. What guards you also draws blood from the one who tends it.

Past the hedge the ground opens onto a still lagoon, and your face lies there on the water, whole where the skin was caught. Mannaz is that meeting of the eye and its own reflection. When the wind combs the surface, which face do you follow, the one that holds or the one that scatters?

You are climbing the mountain path, and beside you a second horse keeps your pace, hoof for hoof up the loose scree. Ehwaz is that matched stride, two moving as one without either pulling ahead. Neither watches the other's face now, both are watching the ground rise. The two who studied their reflection are walking the same slope, Anna, and the climbing needs no mirror.

A single root pushes down through packed earth and hard stone, past every grey layer, until it reaches the water beneath. Then the stones fade, and only that root remains, splitting rock to drink. Nauthiz is the slow pressure that turns being held back into the strength to break through. What stands between you and the water, Anna, that you have not yet leaned your whole weight against?

The lamps are lit while the pot still simmers, and the room warms with voices before a single plate is set down. This, Anna, is Wunjo — the gladness that gathers people before there is any reason given for it. Are you listening to the room, or waiting for the food?

Beyond the small ring of lamplight the workshop stands dark, and the rest of the piece waits there unshaped. Kenaz is that one warm circle where the blade meets the grain and the shavings curl away, thin and pale. It does not light the whole room, only the width of the bench. You are working in the small lit part, with your hands, one cut at a time.

Notice the thin green flush over the seed-bed, days before a single shoot breaks the soil. Ingwaz is that quiet work below, the roots taking hold where no eye reaches yet. What is forming in you keeps its own pace, unhurried by the surface. The greening comes first, Anna, and the rest follows in its time.

The line runs down past the greening you saw before, Anna, into water too dark to follow. Blank is the water holding what it will give before you know its shape. Down there it waits, and no reading yet can name it.

The moor lies wide and still, Anna, and across it the plover's call carries clear on the breeze. That sound crosses the dark water you followed down, reaching you where the greening began. Ansuz is a voice travelling the open air to find your ear at last. Is the call arriving now, or have you only just turned to hear it?

Notice the thin green flush over the seed-bed, days before a single shoot breaks the soil. Ingwaz is that quiet work below, the roots taking hold where no eye reaches yet. What is forming in you keeps its own pace, unhurried by the surface. The greening comes first, Anna, and the rest follows in its time.

Below the surface, Anna, the water holds nothing you can name yet, only the dark and the line dropping into it. Blank is that stillness before the first pull, the moment nothing has arrived. The water keeps its own counsel, and the line waits.

The plover's call holds steady, Anna, while the wind that carries it shifts and scatters over the heather. This is Ansuz — a sound that finds you across open ground, though the air between never keeps still. You are far off, and still the note arrives whole. Does it reach you as a word, or only as a sound crossing the moor?

The current takes the pebble past your feet and turns it once more before it settles somewhere out of sight. This is Perth, the pebble carried in water toward a resting place no eye has found yet. What lies under the surface keeps moving after you have looked away. Would you know the stone again once the river sets it down?

You stand at the water's edge, Anna, where the fjord lies flat and grey and the bird on the rock has not moved since you came. Isa is the world holding its breath, everything paused where it fell. Beneath the still surface the deep water stays dark and unread. Nothing here asks to be hurried on.

You stand at the bank at dawn and the river has risen in the night, brown and fast where it was low. Hagalaz is that rising, the water taking whatever was left too close to the edge. What was near the bank yesterday is gone, and the ground where it sat is bare now. What did you leave standing there?

Hail rakes the June hayfield, bends the grass flat, then clears before the sky does. Hagalaz is the brief violence that comes and goes while the field stays rooted. What in you, Anna, is measuring the damage before the ground has even dried?

A single drop on the smallest stone catches the light and holds it, the part your eye would pass over. This is Sowilo, Anna, the way clear sight lands on one plain thing and makes it visible. The whole field of wet stones is shining now.

See the down still clinging to the youngest one, too small to have found its feet. Berkana is the sheltering warmth that walks life to the water's edge and no further. The eider does not carry them in, she only shows the way and stands close. You are at the water with the whole small brood, watching the first of them slip from the bank.

A single grain of black sand turns in the grey water, so small no eye would follow it down. This, Anna, is what Laguz does — it moves everything the current holds, the fine grit along with the stones. What travels in that water below the surface?

The second cup sits filled, its steam already thinned to nothing. Gebo is that, Anna, the giving that only happens when another hand reaches back across the table. The door stands open to the grey morning and the chair opposite waits, pulled out. You are sitting with coffee poured for two.

The midnight sun hangs low over the fjord, Anna, gilding the water, the fells, the sleepless birds, and then all of it dims but that one steady light on the horizon. Sowilo is the burning that will not set when everything else asks to rest. Which will you follow, the wide gold everywhere, or the one point it comes from?

Behind the two horses climbing the ridge lies the trust worn in over many miles, the reading of each other no rider sees. This is Ehwaz, Anna, the matched stride that lets two carry more than one. Are the horses still keeping pace, or has one begun to lead?

Beneath the loose grey scree, out of sight, one root threads deep and grips the stone. Eihwaz is the hidden hold that keeps the whole slope from sliding when the surface gives way. What looks steady above owes everything to that dark reaching underneath. You stand on the slope, Anna, held by what you cannot see.

A single fern grows from the crack, roots pushed down where no soil should hold. This is Thurisaz, Anna, the edge that will not let you walk straight across. The gap waits, narrow and dark and real. What are you standing at the lip of, waiting for the ground to close?

A single root pushes down through packed earth and hard stone, past every grey layer, until it reaches the water beneath. Then the stones fade, and only that root remains, splitting rock to drink. Nauthiz is the slow pressure that turns being held back into the strength to break through. What stands between you and the water, Anna, that you have not yet leaned your whole weight against?

The lamps go up while the light outside still holds, and the door opens on voices before the pot has come to the boil. This is Wunjo, Anna, the ease of being counted in before you have earned your place at the table. Who is already leaning toward the door, listening for your step on the stones?

Beneath the bench the floor is buried in pale curls, more than one hand could have made in a night. The lamp lights only the blade and the wood parting under it. Kenaz is the making that happens once the doubting stops watching. You are standing over the work, and it is further along than you last looked.

Behind the two horses climbing the ridge lies the trust worn in over many miles, the reading of each other no rider sees. This is Ehwaz, Anna, the matched stride that lets two carry more than one. Are the horses still keeping pace, or has one begun to lead?

Below the track the horses climbed, the yew root grips the loose scree and holds the whole slope from sliding into the gully. This is Eihwaz, the hidden anchor that lets the surface stay standing while everything around it gives way. No one walking the ridge sees the wood that does the holding. You stand on ground that keeps, Anna, over what does not show.

A single black seam runs through the lava, narrow enough to miss underfoot. This is Thurisaz, Anna, the edge that lets nothing across but a jump. The two who climbed together now stand on either side of it. Which foot leaves the ground first?

The road winds along the river and disappears around the next bend, Anna, and everything falls away but that turning. Raidho is the going itself, the ground moving under your feet whether you name the destination or not. You are already walking, and the bend is still ahead.

The rowan stands alone by the farmhouse, roots deep in the black earth, its crown leaning where the wind has always pushed. It gives to the gust but never all the way, and this is what Eihwaz does — it holds a thing rooted while the top of it bends. Everything falls away now but that unbroken line down through the soil, Anna. The tree stays.

The sheepdog lies on the rise where the whole flock stays within its eye, ears turned, nothing hurried. This is Algiz, Anna, the steady watching that lets everything below graze in peace. You are on the high ground now, holding the field in view.

See the single split in the rowan's bark, low down where the wind works hardest. Eihwaz is the wood that gives a little and holds, root deep in the cold ground beneath the farmhouse. You stand at its base, in the shade it keeps.

The two horses climb the ridge together, matching stride for stride where the path narrows. Ehwaz is that trust between them, one setting the pace and the other holding it without falling back. You are on the mountain with another, moving at the same speed.

The egg lies whole in the nest, warm under the down, and nothing of what waits inside shows yet. Ingwaz is that quiet gathering before anything breaks the shell. You are sitting with the nest, and the hour has not come.

The current takes the pebble past your feet and turns it once more before it settles somewhere out of sight. This is Perth, the pebble carried in water toward a resting place no eye has found yet. What lies under the surface keeps moving after you have looked away. Would you know the stone again once the river sets it down?

You stand at the water's edge, Anna, and the fjord holds flat and grey where the current once turned that stone. Nothing stirs now, not even the bird on the rock. Isa is the water gone still enough to hold its own reflection whole. What was moving beneath the surface has come to rest, and the rest keeps its shape.

You wake to the river up past the grass that held it yesterday, and the bank where the still water lay is gone under brown flood. Hagalaz is the night that takes back what looked settled and moves it before you can reach it. The reflection you knew is torn, and the current runs where nothing ran before. What did you leave close to the edge, thinking the water would stay where it stood?

You stand at the thorn hedge, close enough that the barbs catch your sleeve. Thurisaz is the edge that lets nothing through without taking something first. Every gap in the branches asks a price of skin or patience before it opens. What guards you also draws blood from the one who tends it.

Where the water goes still, your face lies clear on its surface, then a breath of wind runs across and the edges begin to move. Mannaz is that seeing of yourself in the calm before the surface stirs. Do you wait for the water to settle, or watch how the ripple changes the shape?

You are on the track up the mountain, and beside you a second horse matches your stride, hoof for hoof over the loose stones. Neither one leads, neither one lags. This is Ehwaz, the trust that lets two move as one across hard ground. The path is steep, Anna, and you climb it side by side.

Before anyone crosses the threshold, the second cup already stands filled, steam thinning in the quiet air. Gebo is that place set at the table before the guest arrives. You are standing in the open doorway, coffee poured, the chair across from you still empty.

The old farmstead stands roofless now, turf walls sunk into grass, yet the hearthstones still hold the shape of every fire lit there. Othila is what an old house keeps long after the people go. Which stones would you carry forward, Anna, and which would you leave in the grass?

The sheepdog lies on the rise where the whole flock spreads below, every ewe held in one steady gaze. Then the far ridge, the fence line, the empty pasture — all of it falls away, and only the flock remains. Algiz is that watching that keeps what matters within sight. The chair filled, the stones chosen, all of it gathered now under one quiet eye.

Under the standing grass the moisture holds, not yet gone from the stalk though the sun has been on it all day. Jera is that waiting the cut hay does, drying in its own time before the blade comes. Do you watch the field, or the light moving over it?

Where the open heath tips into shade, the bilberries hang darkest and thickest by August. This is Fehu, Anna, the slow filling of a thing until it is ready for the hand that gathers it. What ripened all summer waits now on the low branches.

Where the water meets the earth, Anna, the line that held all night is gone by morning. The river has risen and taken the bank whole, everything that stood too near now moving downstream. This is Hagalaz, the sudden pull that carries off what you thought was fixed ground. What the water takes, it does not set back.

The rock beneath holds its old hardness while moss creeps green across every hollow and crack. This is Uruz, the slow work of one form settling over the shape of what came before. The fire is spent, and the field goes on growing over it.

You stand at the crack in the lava, Anna, black rock split wide and no bridge across it. Thurisaz is that edge where standing still and moving both cost you something. What waits on the far side that keeps you here, weighing the jump?

Beneath the stones, where no eye follows, the root is pressing down toward water it cannot yet reach. This is Nauthiz, the slow labour of pushing through what does not give way. What is growing in you, Anna, under weight you never asked to carry?

Under the standing grass the moisture holds, not yet gone from the stalk though the sun has been on it all day. Jera is that waiting the cut hay does, drying in its own time before the blade comes. Do you watch the field, or the light moving over it?

Where the mown field gives way to open heath, the bilberries have come in dark and heavy this month. Fehu is that fullness ripening on the branch, Anna, weight the plant made from sun and slow days. The berries hang where the light left them.

Where the grass held its moisture and the berries hung heavy, Anna, the river came up in the night and took the bank they grew on. Hagalaz is that water pulling the ground out from under what stood too near the edge. The roots that held now hang loose in the current. What the slow days made, one night unmade.

The doorway stays calm, Anna, while the wind tears at the grass on the far side of the wall. That turf bank is Algiz, the standing thing that takes the weather so a quiet space can hold behind it. Everything outside moves, and the still air by the threshold does not. What are you keeping sheltered in that stillness?

The bird on the rock does not move, and the fjord holds the sky without a ripple. This is Isa, the pause where nothing is asked and nothing given. What has gone this quiet in you because it is resting, and what because it stopped?

The walls of the room hold their place, but the light across them is not the light you closed your eyes to. Dagaz is that quiet crossing where dark gives over to day without a single sound. You wake into a morning already changed.

The line drops down into dark water and the surface holds still around it. Blank is the water before anything takes the hook, the space where nothing has yet decided its shape. What lies under the surface stays hidden, and the line waits without pulling. Do you sit with the stillness, or do you let the line drift wider?

Where the still water was, hail now rakes the June hayfield and is gone before the sky clears. Hagalaz is the hard weather that flattens the grass and passes without asking. What stands up again once the ice has melted into the ground?

One thin thread of mirrored cloud shivers at the water's edge, the part the eye slides past. Mannaz is the face the still lagoon gives back, clear until the smallest breath crosses it. The hail flattened the field and the hook waited under the dark, and now the surface holds a likeness of the sky above it. Do you read the water for what it shows, or the wind that keeps moving it?

Beyond the lamp's small circle the workshop sits dark, Anna, and the shape you are making is still hidden in the wood. Kenaz is that steady light held close over the work, enough to see the next cut and no further. The shavings curl away and fall, and the form comes out slowly under the blade. You cannot light the whole room, only the bench where your hands are.

Beyond the shoulder of the hill the sheep-track keeps on where you cannot yet see it, Anna, worn smooth by hooves that followed the easiest ground. Raidho is that steady going that finds its own pace without being driven. Where does the track lead your eye, over the rise or down toward the shore?

The walls of the room are where they always were, but the light has already turned while you slept. Dagaz is that first grey giving way to gold, the shift you did not stand watch for. Nothing moved except the hour, and the hour moved everything. You are lying still in a room that is no longer the one you closed your eyes in.

Hail rakes the June hayfield, bends the grass flat, then clears before the sky does. Hagalaz is the brief violence that comes and goes while the field stays rooted. What in you, Anna, is measuring the damage before the ground has even dried?

On one stone at the field's edge, a single drop holds the whole sky and shines. Sowilo is the light that finds the wet places first, Anna, and warms them dry. The field steams a little now, and stands.

The last duckling waits at the edge, one webbed foot testing the water before the rest follow. Berkana is the tending that goes out ahead, holding the small ones close until they can hold themselves. The eider does not push, she simply goes in, and they come. You are the one already in the water now, and the others are watching your feet.

You wake, and the grey of the room has already gone gold at its edges without your noticing. Dagaz is that hinge, Anna, where night has finished and the day is not yet named. What did the dark become while you were not watching for it?

The gold that touched the room's edge has climbed, Anna, and now it lies across the whole hayfield at midnight, so the grass never gives up its colour to dark. Sowilo is that light that will not set, holding the field lit long past the hour of sleep. The scythes rest, but the cut rows stay warm. What was named at dawn keeps its brightness through the night.

You stand where the wave slides up the black sand and pulls back, leaving the shore wet and taking a little of it out with each draw. Gebo is that trade the sea and the land keep without counting, one motion feeding both. Nothing here is only given, nothing only kept. You are at the tideline, where the water arrives and leaves in the same breath.

Rain runs down the guide-stone and off its edges, and the stone holds the same line it held before the sky opened. This is Tiwaz, Anna, the weight that keeps one direction whatever falls on it. Water finds the low ground, but the marker stays true. What in you refuses to lean when the pressure comes down?

The nest holds still while the grass around it moves in the wind. The egg lies whole and warm, and nothing of what it carries shows on its shell. Ingwaz is the quiet gathering that keeps before it opens, taking its own time. You stand at the nest's edge, Anna, watching what has not yet broken.

You stand at the gate as the sheep drift in toward evening, slow and heavy with the day, needing no driving now. Fehu is the worth that comes home on its own feet when the season has done its work, Anna. What has been out grazing all summer walks back toward you now, unhurried. Which of them do you count in as they pass?

The whole valley lies under grey until the sun cracks it open, and then it is only this: light glinting on the wet stones at your feet. Sowilo is that sudden clearing, when seeing gathers to one bright point. Which stone holds the glint you keep coming back to?

The room, the window, the phone in your hand, and a voice saying the thing you have waited to hear — and then only the voice. Ansuz is the moment a message crosses the air and finally lands where it was meant to. Everything else in the room goes quiet around those words. You are holding the phone, hearing them arrive.

The scree shifts loose down the slope, small stones going with it, and one root holds fast through the middle of it all. This is what Eihwaz does, Anna, it keeps a footing while the ground gives way. The stones move but the root does not follow them down. What stays gripped in the earth while the loose things run?

The road winds along the river and disappears around the next bend, Anna, and everything falls away but that turning. Raidho is the going itself, the ground moving under your feet whether you name the destination or not. You are already walking, and the bend is still ahead.

The road that turned at the bend brings you here, to the rowan standing alone by the farmhouse, its trunk leaning hard against the wind but never all the way over. Eihwaz is what holds in the roots while the crown gives ground. The bending is not the breaking, and the tree knows the difference. It has stood here a long time, Anna, and it stands here still.

The sheepdog lies on the rise, the whole flock spread below, then the world narrows to its steady watching. Algiz is that keeping-watch that holds a wide field in one gaze, Anna. You are the dog on the rise, and the flock is all below you.

Before anyone crosses the threshold, the second cup already stands filled, steam thinning in the quiet air. Gebo is that place set at the table before the guest arrives. You are standing in the open doorway, coffee poured, the chair across from you still empty.

The old farmstead stands roofless in the grass, walls open to the sky, yet the hearthstone still marks where warmth once gathered. Othila is that warmth carried forward long after the roof is gone. Which stones do you keep, Anna, and which do you let the grass take back?

The sheepdog lies on the rise where the whole flock spreads below it, every ewe within its watching. Then the field falls away, and only that steady seeing remains. Algiz is the eye that holds the edges of what matters, keeping watch so the middle can graze in peace. Nothing needs guarding that is not already seen.

A single grain of black sand turns in the grey water, so small no eye would follow it down. This, Anna, is what Laguz does — it moves everything the current holds, the fine grit along with the stones. What travels in that water below the surface?

The second cup sits filled, its steam thinning into the cool air. This is what Gebo does, Anna, it lays a place before the guest arrives and asks nothing of them yet. The current you watched below the water has carried someone to your door. You are standing in the open doorway, coffee warm on the table for two.

The whole valley lies lit at midnight, Anna, the fell, the water, the two cups on the sill all holding the same low gold. This is what Sowilo does, it keeps the light on long past the hour it should have gone. Now everything dims but the far ridge — what is it up there that still catches the sun?

The rock beneath holds its old hardness while moss creeps green across every hollow and crack. This is Uruz, the slow work of one form settling over the shape of what came before. The fire is spent, and the field goes on growing over it.

You stand at the crack in the lava, Anna, black rock split wide where the moss stops short of the edge. This is Thurisaz, the gap that will not be walked across, only jumped. What are you still measuring on this side of it?

Below the split rock a root works down through packed stone, pushing where there is no room, toward water it cannot yet see. This is Nauthiz, the pressing on that only hard ground teaches. What holds you, Anna, is also what is teaching your reach to go deeper?

Rain runs down the guide-stone and off its edges, and the stone holds the same line it held before the sky opened. This is Tiwaz, Anna, the weight that keeps one direction whatever falls on it. Water finds the low ground, but the marker stays true. What in you refuses to lean when the pressure comes down?

The rain has passed, and where the stone stood firm the nest now sits sheltered under the low branch. The egg lies whole inside it, warm, and nothing of what it holds shows on the shell. This is Ingwaz, the gathered thing that waits under its own quiet for its hour to come. You are standing beside the nest, Anna, keeping watch over what has not yet opened.

You stand at the fold as the light goes soft, and the sheep come in one after another, unhurried. Each one carries the summer's grass in its own weight now, Anna, the fat of good grazing turned to something you can count. This is Fehu, the season's keeping walking home on four legs. Do you open the gate wide, or hold some back on the hill?

Beyond the lamp's small circle the workshop sits dark, Anna, and the shape you are making is still hidden in the wood. Kenaz is that steady light held close over the work, enough to see the next cut and no further. The shavings curl away and fall, and the form comes out slowly under the blade. You cannot light the whole room, only the bench where your hands are.

Beyond the workshop door, Anna, the sheep-track winds along the hillside without anyone laying it. Raidho is that path found by walking, worn by many feet before yours. The going is neither fast nor slow, only its own pace. Do you set the pace, or does the track already hold it?

The bed under you is the same, and the walls where you always find them, but the light in the room has already changed while you slept. Dagaz is that grey turning to grey-gold at the edges, the shift you did not stay awake for. You do not see the sun cross the sill, only the room it leaves behind. You are lying in the room that morning has already reached.

The phone rings, and a voice carries the words you have waited for across the quiet room. Then everything falls away but the sound of that voice. Ansuz is the moment a message finds the ear it was meant for — will you hold it as spoken, or ask it to say more?

See the split bark low on the trunk, the scar most eyes pass over. The rowan by the farmhouse leans hard in the west wind yet never bends the whole way down. Eihwaz is the hold that keeps a thing standing when the weight comes from beneath. That old wood took the storm and stayed rooted, Anna.

The pace between them holds, though the mountain steepens and the loose scree slides underfoot. Two horses climb as one, each matching the other's stride without a rein to hold it there. Ehwaz is the trust that lets two carry a weight neither would climb alone. You are moving up the track beside another, step for step.

You wake, and the grey of the room has already gone gold at its edges without your noticing. Dagaz is that hinge, Anna, where night has finished and the day is not yet named. What did the dark become while you were not watching for it?

Where the day should have ended, Anna, the light stays on the cut hay and the field goes on glowing well past bedtime. Sowilo is that warmth that does not know when to stop, the sun refusing the usual boundary. What was meant to close instead keeps giving. The grass lies bright under a sky that never quite darkens.

You stand where the water reaches the sand and pulls back again in one motion, foam left behind, small stones drawn under. This is Gebo, the giving and the taking that come as a single breath, not two. What arrives here does not stay, and what goes out returns changed. You are standing in the wet line where the sea meets the shore.

The turf wall settles year by year, Anna, its grass roof folding back into the ground the forefathers took it from. Othila is that slow return of what was built to what holds it. You stand where the old line goes green again.

The pale line along the far wall has shifted since you closed your eyes, thin and grey where it was dark. Dagaz is that quiet turn the night makes into morning, seen only if you catch it. You wake into a room already changed, though nothing in it has moved. Do you watch the light come, or turn back toward the dark you knew?

The ewe stands still in the green field while her lambs try their legs beside her, wobbling over ground they have never touched. Berkana is that first walk taken on unsteady feet, held up by nothing but the wish to move. The grass is wet and the light is new, and the lambs do not wait to feel ready. You are standing in that same open field, Anna, on legs still finding their ground.

The line drops down into dark water and the surface holds still around it. Blank is the water before anything takes the hook, the space where nothing has yet decided its shape. What lies under the surface stays hidden, and the line waits without pulling. Do you sit with the stillness, or do you let the line drift wider?

Where the green field ends the hail begins, white and hard on the standing grass, then gone before the cloud has passed. This is Hagalaz, the brief violence that flattens what was growing and leaves the ground bare and cold. What did that short battering strip away that will not stand again?

See the single reed at the lagoon's edge, doubled in the water below it. Mannaz is the way a face knows itself only in the still surface that holds it. Then a breath of wind moves across, and the reflection shivers into loose light. Does the picture on the water break, or is it only learning how the wind touches it?
